title: The future tense of regular verbs
topic: the future tense (pa'al): prefixes and endings
why: After the past, here is the future tense of regular verbs: four prefixes to remember and three endings, so you can talk about your plans. It's the gateway to the "Plans and the Future" unit, which will then add the near future, compound nouns, and pi'el.

The future: it all happens up front

In the past, you added an ending to the verb: כָּתַבְתִּי (I wrote). In the future, it's mainly the beginning that changes: a prefix attaches to the front of the root כ־ת־ב (to write), a bit like English \"will\" coming before \"write.\" For three persons (feminine \"you,\" plural \"you,\" and \"they\"), you also add an ending.

PronounFuturePronunciationMeaning
אֲנִיאֶכְתֹּבekhtovI will write
אַתָּהתִּכְתֹּבtikhtovyou will write (m.)
אַתְּתִּכְתְּבִיtikhteviyou will write (f.)
הוּאיִכְתֹּבyikhtovhe will write
הִיאתִּכְתֹּבtikhtovshe will write
אֲנַחְנוּנִכְתֹּבnikhtovwe will write
אַתֶּם / אַתֶּןתִּכְתְּבוּtikhtevuyou (pl.) will write
הֵם / הֵןיִכְתְּבוּyikhtevuthey will write

The four prefixes: אֶ (I), תִּ (you, she, you plural), יִ (he, they), נִ (we). Their letters, א י ת נ, spell the name אֵיתָן (Eitan): that's the memory trick Israeli schoolchildren use.

As in the past, the pronoun is optional in the 1st and 2nd person: מָחָר אֶכְתֹּב (tomorrow I'll write). With he, she, and they, keep the subject.

", "

Future-tense traps

One form, two meanings. תִּכְתֹּב means \"you will write\" (to a man) and \"she will write.\" The pronoun or the situation decides: אַתָּה תִּכְתֹּב, הִיא תִּכְתֹּב.

O or a? Many verbs have an o in the future, like אֶכְתֹּב. Others have an a: לִלְמֹד (to study) gives אֶלְמַד. There's no simple rule: learn the vowel together with the verb.

PronounFuturePronunciationMeaning
אֲנִיאֶלְמַדelmadI will study
אַתָּהתִּלְמַדtilmadyou will study (m.)
אַתְּתִּלְמְדִיtilmediyou will study (f.)
הוּאיִלְמַדyilmadhe will study
הִיאתִּלְמַדtilmadshe will study
אֲנַחְנוּנִלְמַדnilmadwe will study
אַתֶּם / אַתֶּןתִּלְמְדוּtilmeduyou (pl.) will study
הֵם / הֵןיִלְמְדוּyilmeduthey will study

The same goes for לִלְבֹּשׁ (to wear): אֶלְבַּשׁ, תִּלְבְּשִׁי. For אַתֶּן and הֵן, spoken Hebrew uses the same forms as the masculine.

In speech, you'll often hear אֲנִי יִכְתֹּב instead of אֲנִי אֶכְתֹּב. It's very colloquial: say אֶכְתֹּב. Verbs that begin with a guttural (לַעֲבֹד, לֶאֱכֹל) have slightly different vowels: we'll see them later.

", "

Talking about your plans

A few expressions to place your plans in time: מָחָר (tomorrow), בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ (this weekend), בַּשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא (next week), בַּשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה (next year).

בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ אֶפְגֹּשׁ חֲבֵרִים.This weekend, I'll meet up with friends. [be-sof ha-shavu'a efgosh khaverim]
בַּשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה הִיא תִּלְמַד בְּחֵיפָה.Next year, she'll study in Haifa. [ba-shana ha-ba'a hi tilmad be-Kheifa]
מָתַי תִּגְמְרוּ לַעֲבֹד?When will you (pl.) finish working? [matay tigmeru la'avod?]

הַבָּא agrees like an adjective: שָׁבוּעַ is masculine, so הַשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא; שָׁנָה is feminine, so הַשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה.

As in English (\"tomorrow I'm leaving\"), the present also works for a near, certain future: מָחָר אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ לְאֵילַת (tomorrow I'm going to Eilat).
